messages.author: 5265a29ef692b9d2
messages.subject: Which analysis should I use?
parts:
Hi!

First of all, thanks for providing ezpackage, this is really great!
However, as ezpackage is giving me so many options, I'm wondering now,
which implementation is right for my setting:

I have 4 different groups (treatments) with 50 participants each. Each
participant's action is observed 5 times under the same condition. I
get the 5 values within one "round", where each participant has to
click 5 times at arbitrary moments.
I know that the different values for each participant are not
independent of each other. However, time effects are not of interest
for me and I don't assume that learning effects are apparent. I just
monitor 5 values for each participant in order to get more data. All
the data within one group (for all users) is then taken together and
an aggregated measure is calculated. Now the question is, whether
there are significant differences for this measure between the groups.
As there is no unbiased estimator for the measure and as my data is
not normal, I know that I need some form of sampling.

I've got two main questions:
First, I'm not sure whether bootstrapping or permutation tests seem to
be more appropriate.
Second, could I "ignore" the repeated measures and permute all values
together without regard to the participants who provided it? If not,
could I take vectors for each participant or user vector norms
instead?

What happens if I have an unbalanced design (when some answers are
missing)?

Thank you so much for your help!
Patricia

messages.author: 265b547d9e4946a9
messages.subject: Re: Which analysis should I use?
parts:
ANOVA don't require the data to be normal - just the residuals of the
model. It can be problematic to ignore the repeated measures - not
least because you would lose information and statistical power. It can
also introduce biases in some cases.

I'd start with RM ANOVA and look at residual plots ... and maybe
consider a transformation. Not familiar with the permutation options
yet ... these are tricky for repeated measures and I'm not sure how ez
does it.

Thom
